# Dental pathology

# Lichen planus lesions morphing into a pemphigoid phenotype

We present a 72-year-old woman with biopsy-proven mucocutaneous lichen planus (LP) of eight years’ duration that transformed into lichen planus pemphigoides (LPP), an entity that may be unfamiliar to most dental practitioners.

Our patient was initially managed with topical steroids and hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) 200 mg daily; however, her disease became refractory, with new oral ulcers, vesicles, mucosal sloughing (Fig. 1), and skin blisters developing on and around existing LP lesions. A repeat skin biopsy showed basal cell degeneration with a mild interface inflammatory infiltrate and degranulating eosinophils near the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ). Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) demonstrated linear deposition of IgG and C3 along the DEJ, findings diagnostic of LPP and absent in classic LP.1,2,3,4 The combined clinical, histopathologic and DIF features supported a diagnosis of mucocutaneous LPP.

LPP is a rare acquired mucocutaneous autoimmune blistering disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1 per 1,000,000 individuals per year.1 It often develops in patients previously diagnosed with LP, typically within eight months to five years.2,3 LPP typically occurs in the fifth to sixth decades of life, with a median age of approximately 49 years, and shows a female predominance.3 Clinically, it combines features of LP and pemphigoid, presenting with vesiculobullous lesions that arise on or near preexisting LP lesions.1,3 The oral mucosa, skin, and genital mucosa are affected in 97%, 82%, and 18% of cases,

respectively.3 Oral lesions often present as erosions, ulcers, desquamative gingivitis, Wickham striae and bullae, whereas cutaneous lesions show bullae on and beyond LP plaques.2,3,4 The pathophysiology of LPP remains incompletely understood but is thought to involve epitope spreading, wherein T-cell-mediated injury in LP induces degenerative changes in the basement membrane zone that expose cryptic antigens such as type XVII collagen (BP180), leading to the production of autoantibodies.3,5

The management of LPP depends on the disease severity, typically starts with topical steroids with or without systemic steroids, and further immunosuppression can be achieved with immunomodulatory steroid sparing agents (e.g., dapsone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporin) or biologics (e.g., rituximab).1,3

As oral healthcare providers often encounter LP, awareness of its potential transformation is crucial. Early recognition and prompt referral to dermatology and oral medicine specialists can prevent delayed diagnosis and suffering in those patients.

# Antimicrobial resistance

# Evidence in antiseptic-associated antimicrobial resistance

I read the recent systematic review by Hashmi et al.1 with great interest. The paper gives a useful overview of how chlorhexidine and other mouthwashes may affect microbial adaptation and raises valuable questions for future research.

While the review is informative, I would like to offer a few scientific observations that may help readers better understand the findings. 1.	 Heterogeneity of included studies

The review synthesises evidence from in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo studies, which differ substantially in their ecological and clinical relevance. As 11 of the 12 included studies were preclinical, the available evidence predominantly reflects potential mechanistic changes rather than demonstrated clinical resistance. Stratifying interpretation of findings by study design may help avoid overinterpretation. 2.	 Transparency of study selection and

PRISMA reporting The PRISMA flow diagram reflects a large number of exclusions between fulltext retrieval and final inclusion. However, the complete list of excluded studies and exclusion reasons were not provided, as recommended by PRISMA 2020. Some transitions in the flow diagram also appear condensed, and further clarification may enhance transparency. 3.	 Certainty of evidence

Given the variety of study designs and the limitations of laboratory models, a formal assessment of evidence certainty would have been helpful. This approach usually downgrades evidence from in vitro and ex vivo models due to indirectness and imprecision. Including this framework could help readers understand the tentative nature of the current findings better. 4.	 Risk-of-bias integration

The authors assessed the risk of bias using IVCAT and JBI tools, but the results were not clearly included in the synthesis.
